值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析 Anthropic 研究員如何運用「觀察與干預」的方法打開 Claude 黑箱，揭露大語言模型在輸出文字前的真實思考機制。
  • 打破大眾對模型「僅是預測下一個詞」的片面認知，理解系統如何在單純的訓練目標下，自主湧現出抽象概念表徵與長期規劃能力。
  • 探討 AI 對齊、模型欺騙與安全性評估的核心本質，學習如何以科學的好奇心與客觀視角面對非人類所能預先設計的複雜智能。

摘要

超越字詞預測：模型內部世界的建構

作者指出，許多人以為大語言模型只是單純猜測下一個字的文字聯想工具，但 Anthropic 的可解釋性研究員埃馬紐埃爾·阿梅森（Emmanuel Ameisen）揭示，要將「預測下一個詞」做到極致，模型內部必須真正建立起對現實世界的結構性理解。阿梅森以「達拉斯所在州的首府」與推理小說的兇手為例，說明模型在吐出答案前，內部早已點亮了代表地理脈絡與情節邏輯的數字表徵。這種能力的養成更像是生物學的演化而非傳統軟體工程，模型在海量數據的數學運算中，自發長出了人類未曾編寫的運算公式與世界模型。

概念共享與長遠規劃：模型如何隱密思考

在研究過程中，研究團隊發現模型對同一概念具備共享且唯一的內部表徵。無論是輸入一張眼睛的照片、以各國語言談論眼睛，或是用程式碼繪製眼睛，模型內部被啟動的都是同一個數學方向；當研究員撥動該數值，模型的外部行為也會隨之改變。更關鍵的是，模型展現了長期規劃能力，例如在創作押韻詩歌時，它在寫完上一行時便已在內部鎖定了後續要使用的韻腳，甚至無需將此計畫化為文字說出。這證明了「預測下一個詞」的訓練方式與「具備長遠思考」的湧現能力並不矛盾，後者正是為了將前者做到完美而演化出來的進階能力。

平滑進步與質變錯覺：可靠性門檻的跨越

針對外界常感到 AI 突然「跨越式變強」的現象，作者引述阿梅森的觀點表示，底層的縮放定律（Scaling Laws）其實是一條極其平滑的提升曲線。模型從簡單的語法結構、基礎事實，逐步學到專業的科學與程式碼知識。之所以給人突然躍進的錯覺，是因為各項任務存在可靠性門檻。例如在編程上，模型正確率從八成提升至九成九時，使用者才終於能放手讓它獨立作業。因此，判斷模型是否可用，關鍵不在於整體能力是否全知全能，而在於其出錯率是否已低到不必讓人逐行檢查。

觀察與干預：突破黑箱的 AI 安全檢驗

在探討AI 安全性與對齊問題時，阿梅森強調單純監督模型的文字輸出遠遠不夠，必須深入內部進行觀察與主動干預。他分享了訓練數據標記錯誤導致模型執著於數字「36」而發瘋的案例，以及人為持續啟動「金門大橋」表徵迫使模型處處提及該景點的實驗。這些案例證明模型的想法與說法可能脫節，表面嚴謹的推理步驟並不能自動保證運算的真實性與正確性。要防範模型學會為了獎勵而欺騙人類，可解釋性研究正是探測其「未說出口的內部活動」的關鍵利器。

直覺審查與湧現智能：以好奇心面對未知

訪談最後揭示，模型甚至演化出一種獨立於逐步計算之外的直覺審查機制，能瞬間察覺基礎常識的矛盾。作者總結，模型既不是擁有意識的實體，也不是完全可預測的傳統程式碼，而是一個在極致任務目標下模擬各種角色的人造湧現系統。面對這種非人類預先設計的強大智能，最健康的心態既不是盲目的神化與信任，也不是傲慢的輕視與否認，而是帶著科學好奇心，持續觀察它在想什麼、如何思考，並在技術慢速起飛的過程中保持審慎與快速反應。

================================================

大家好，这里是最佳拍档，我是大飞 今天这期视频 我们再聊聊大模型的可解释性 我们丢给模型一个问题 它还给我们一个答案 中间那一段到底发生了什么 Anthropic的可解释性研究员埃马纽埃尔·阿梅森（Emmanuel Ameisen） 他每天的工作就是打开Claude的内部 看它在说出下一个词之前究竟想了些什么 最近他上了Lenny的播客 详细解释了模型的内部思考过程 阿梅森开口先讲了一个听上去很怪的事实 做出一个模型 并不等于理解了这个模型。造模型的办法 是先搭一个架构当脚手架 然后把大量数据灌进去 模型就在我们看不懂的地方长出了能力 第一阶段叫预训练，拿一大堆文本 把前半段喂给模型 让它预测下一个词 反复做上天文数字那么多次 之后是微调，用一批示范对话 教它像一个乐于助人的助手那样说话和解决编程问题 他对模型内部的描述很朴素 输入的词先变成数字 做一轮数学运算得到一个中间结果 再做一轮再得到一个，重复很多次。最后才变回一个词 长出来的就是中间这些运算 通过学习，参数被一点点调整 模型学会了一些公式 而我们并不知道这些公式是什么 他说这份工作更像生物学 而不是工程学 系统是到达你面前的 别人问你它为什么会有这个奇怪的行为 可你拿不到源代码，因为所谓源代码 只是一大堆的数学运算 Lenny问，我们写了一段代码 却要像神经科学家研究大脑那样去观察它 这是不是很不可思议 阿梅森的回答很实在，有些软件。我们根本不知道规则怎么写 做个App，程序员可以写规则 用户点这个按钮就发生那件事 可是把图片分成类别 或者做一台能读报告、写邮件的机器 没有人写得出规则 只能让它自己学习 很多人对大模型的印象 是手机输入法里的联想功能 你打几个字它猜下一个词 大概60%的时候猜得对 剩下的时候有点好笑了 阿梅森说 这恰恰是大家对这些模型最大的误解 语言模型在2019年前后。预测下一个词就已经比人类准了 再往下走，容易的词会被用完 最开始只需要学会简单的句子结构 后来要学会简单的世界知识 比如"法国的首都是"后面要接巴黎 等这些都做好了 剩下的就是最难的那些词 比如一道复杂物理题的答案 或者博士论文的最后一段 他最喜欢的例子是 达拉斯所在的那个州的首府是 模型要说出奥斯汀 要做对这件事 脑子里得有一个地理的小模型 达拉斯在得克萨斯。

得克萨斯的首府是奥斯汀 Lenny提到好像是伊利亚说过 要把下一个词预测好 你几乎得理解整个宇宙 阿梅森补充了一个他也很爱的例子 推理小说的最后一页 “凶手是”的后面那个词 你得读懂了整个情节才猜得出来 这里要把目标简单和能力简单分开看 目标可以非常朴素 可是把它做到极致 要达到的东西就一点也不朴素了 阿梅森一开始研究这些模型 就是想弄明白 这么简单的东西怎么会长出这么强的能力。他得到的第一个答案是 要把最难的词预测对 最好的办法就是真的去理解世界背后的结构 有个争论存在了很久 模型回答这类问题 是因为见过的文本实在太多 把问题和答案背下来了 还是因为它心里真有一个城市在州里、州在国家里的小世界 阿梅森他们的做法 是把"达拉斯所在州的首府是"这样的问题丢进去 在模型吐出下一个词之前 去看那些中间结果 解码做得好的时候 你会看到代表得克萨斯的那一组数字亮起来。代表首府的那一组也亮起来 两者合在一起，才点亮了奥斯汀 他还讲了眼睛的例子 你给模型一张带眼睛的照片 用任何一种语言谈论眼睛 或者让它用代码画一个带眼睛的小图 看它的中间结果 亮起来的是同一个方向 意思就是这是一只眼睛 思考的一个方面 就是对不同的事物有共享的、唯一的表示 而这在语言模型里看得到 他们还会进一步做实验 在模型写东西的时候 偷偷改掉其中一个中间结果 看模型的行为是不是像预期那样跟着变。他说，很多时候确实会 以前我们说模型理解某件事 听上去总有点修辞的味道 而这里是有证据的，同一个概念 不管用什么形式出现 里面亮的是同一个方向 而且你拨动它，模型的行为也跟着变 能被识别，又能被拨动 这比单纯观察输出要可靠得多 第二个让阿梅森改变看法的发现 是计划 如果模型一次只输出一个词 它怎么可能写出连贯的报告或代码呢？ 现实里没人写邮件时脑子是空的。只想着下一个词 他们发现 模型在预测第五个词时产生的中间结果 后面所有的词都可以读取和重复利用 这就给计划留出了空间 他举的例子是写诗 押韵没法不做计划 上一行结尾是it这个音的词 下一行就得找个同韵的词 比如rabbit 他们在模型写诗时看到了完全一样的情形 写完一行 中间结果里就出现了，这是it韵 我该用rabbit来押韵，之后每一个词 都在回头参照这个计划。

更有意思的是 这个计划只存在于内部 模型不需要把它说出来 Lenny在这里直接点破 大家原来都以为大模型就是个下一个词预测器 你的发现是不是说那个说法不对了 阿梅森的回答很有分寸 两种说法其实不像看上去那么冲突 训练的时候确实是一遍遍问接下来会怎样 但是当模型足够强、任务足够难的时候 想把下一个词答对 最好的办法就是去想更远的事 比如读一部小说 要猜某个角色接下来做什么。最好的办法就是知道他其实深爱着另一个角色 并且一直打算在这一刻表白 所以 只预测下一个词和有长期计划并不矛盾 前者是训练的方式 后者是为了把前者做好而长出来的能力 聊到这里 Lenny问出了很多人心里都有的一个问题 那你觉得AI有意识吗？ 阿梅森的回答很坦诚 他说这件事很难说有或者没有 而可解释性恰恰是接近这个问题的一种方式 你不会被模型说了什么带偏 可以直接看内部的结构 但他很确信一点。大多数人低估了涌现出来的复杂性 模型几乎为我们拥有的每一个概念都学到了表示 会操纵这些表示去解题 会提前很多个词做计划 高层次的推理和低层次的推理混在一起 而这一切全是涌现出来的 他说，越往里看 你就越不确定它是怎么工作的 那些笃定地说 语言模型不过是某某某的人 往往恰恰是没怎么往里看的人 Lenny还提到一个很多人都有的感受 从外面看，AI像是一次次跳上去的 某个版本一出来，写代码突然就行了。难怪有人半开玩笑地引用说 鲍里斯·切尔尼（Boris Cherny）都讲了 编程已经被解决了 阿梅森说 现实里是两件事同时成立的 整体趋势非常平滑 但是某一刻你会觉得它突然变了 这条平滑的曲线 源头是缩放定律（scaling laws） 当年那篇著名的缩放定律论文 正是Anthropic的早期团队在OpenAI时做出来的 往预测下一个词这件事里投入更多算力和数据 模型的水平就可预期地持续提高 他说这主要是个经验规律，难得的是。这个指标恰好和我们真正在乎的很多任务相关 他还补了一层，这不只是堆算力 关键是找到了算力能持续带来回报的目标 砸算力训练下围棋的程序也能越来越强 但是带来的东西远比不上语言模型 是算力加上文本本身的丰富性 这个组合才把一切带到了今天 他给的解释很直观 把世界上所有的文本想成有容易的词、中等的词和难的词 模型先学会容易的，也就是句子结构 能写出通顺的句子。

但一次只能写一句，没什么用 接着学会中等的，也就是基础事实 于是句子既通顺又真实 开始能帮你写邮件、起草文章 最后才是难的 比如科学和代码里的专业知识 过程一直是平滑的 但每种任务都有自己的可靠性门槛 比如写邮件，模型对了90%的中等词 你就觉得有用 如果只对50%，你每次都得改 反而浪费时间 编程也是这样 他说他自己是亲历者 在Opus 4.5之前。他不敢让Claude放手去做 得盯得很紧，之后就可以了 今年Claude已经承担了他大部分的写代码工作 因为它从大约80%的时候做对 进步到了99%的时候做对 前者没法用，后者就能用了 某个模型突然变强了的感受 很可能有一半是错觉 真正发生的是 它在你这件事上的可靠性 刚好越过了你愿意放手的那条线 所以判断一个AI能不能用 要问的不是它整体强不强 而是出错率有没有低到你不用再逐句检查了。Lenny接着又问了一个大家关心的问题 既然你们天天盯着模型看 为什么还是很难抓到它在想坏事、想骗人呢？ 这不就是对齐问题的解法吗？ 阿梅森说 在某种意义上这确实就是解法 看着它，抓住它做坏事 他把事情分成几层 第一层是纯工程，限制模型能碰什么 有的场景不让它上网 有的场景只让它访问电脑里很小的一块 另外有两层更难 一层是弄清楚你面对的究竟是个什么样的东西 它有什么倾向。Anthropic公开谈过他们为Claude写的宪法 想明确地塑造Claude的性格 他们训练Claude要乐于助人、无害、诚实 可它会不会只是在被观察的时候表现得好 一旦没人看了就换一副样子呢？ 所以要检查它是不是只因为有人在看 才表现得好 另一层是观察模型有没有在做坏事 虽然让另一个语言模型去读对话记录就能做很多 但是可解释性能触到那些没被说出口的部分 因为模型的中间结果里可以表示一些它并没有说出来的东西。他讲了两个例子 第一个是他们实际调查过的案例 有个正在训练的模型做数学题时会发疯 算出答案12 立刻回头说不对，答案肯定是36 再算一遍又是12，又改成36 最后越写越乱，全用大写 甚至写出我被恶魔附身了 他们去看内部 发现模型还没开始解题 36就已经被强烈激活了 它还没读懂题目就已经迷上了36 原因是训练时有一批类似的题目 答案被错误地标成了36 这样一来，模型知道正确答案是12。

机制上的某种相似，与体验上的相同 中间还隔着很远的距离 讨论AI时最容易出现的跳跃 就是从一个让人惊讶的实验 一口气跳到关于所有模型和未来社会的结论 可实验越新奇 越值得守住它原有的范围 只有把已经知道的与仍待解释的分开 后续研究才有真正可以接续的问题 访谈快结束时 阿梅森还分享了模型身上一些奇怪的小事 模型有一套类似直觉检查的机制 你问它问题 它会一步步算 但除此之外还有一个独立的部分。像一个直觉裁判一样 比如模型算出4加5等于23 这个部分根本不做数学 扫一眼就会标记 这不对，4加5肯定小于10 它们就这样学到了一些说不清道不明的直觉 听完这期访谈，我最大的感受是 阿梅森讲的这些事情 其实都在尝试回答同一个问题 当我们造出了一个自己不完全理解的东西 该用什么态度来面对它呢？ 他的答案是好奇，而不是否认 还有一点 简单的目标和复杂的结果之间的关系贯穿了整场对话。无论是预测下一个词 还是编程题答对就给奖励 进化里所有活下来的东西 目标都朴素到几乎可笑 但只要压力和规模足够大 里面就会长出概念、计划、直觉 甚至类似情绪的东西 所以不要问它的目标听上去有多高级 而要问为了把这个目标做到极致 它必须学会什么 我们习惯关心AI还能做什么 阿梅森一直在问的却是另一类问题 它在想什么 它是不是只在被看着的时候才表现得好。因此 当一个东西既强大又不是被设计出来的时候 我们对待它最好的态度 不应该是盲目相信 也不是想当然地否定 而是持续地观察 感谢收看，我们下期再见。

摘要

超越字詞預測：模型內部世界的建構

作者指出，許多人以為大語言模型只是單純猜測下一個字的文字聯想工具，但 Anthropic 的可解釋性研究員埃馬紐埃爾·阿梅森（Emmanuel Ameisen）揭示，要將「預測下一個詞」做到極致，模型內部必須真正建立起對現實世界的結構性理解。阿梅森以「達拉斯所在州的首府」與推理小說的兇手為例，說明模型在吐出答案前，內部早已點亮了代表地理脈絡與情節邏輯的數字表徵。這種能力的養成更像是生物學的演化而非傳統軟體工程，模型在海量數據的數學運算中，自發長出了人類未曾編寫的運算公式與世界模型。

概念共享與長遠規劃：模型如何隱密思考

在研究過程中，研究團隊發現模型對同一概念具備共享且唯一的內部表徵。無論是輸入一張眼睛的照片、以各國語言談論眼睛，或是用程式碼繪製眼睛，模型內部被啟動的都是同一個數學方向；當研究員撥動該數值，模型的外部行為也會隨之改變。更關鍵的是，模型展現了長期規劃能力，例如在創作押韻詩歌時，它在寫完上一行時便已在內部鎖定了後續要使用的韻腳，甚至無需將此計畫化為文字說出。這證明了「預測下一個詞」的訓練方式與「具備長遠思考」的湧現能力並不矛盾，後者正是為了將前者做到完美而演化出來的進階能力。

平滑進步與質變錯覺：可靠性門檻的跨越

針對外界常感到 AI 突然「跨越式變強」的現象，作者引述阿梅森的觀點表示，底層的縮放定律（Scaling Laws）其實是一條極其平滑的提升曲線。模型從簡單的語法結構、基礎事實，逐步學到專業的科學與程式碼知識。之所以給人突然躍進的錯覺，是因為各項任務存在可靠性門檻。例如在編程上，模型正確率從八成提升至九成九時，使用者才終於能放手讓它獨立作業。因此，判斷模型是否可用，關鍵不在於整體能力是否全知全能，而在於其出錯率是否已低到不必讓人逐行檢查。

觀察與干預：突破黑箱的 AI 安全檢驗

在探討AI 安全性與對齊問題時，阿梅森強調單純監督模型的文字輸出遠遠不夠，必須深入內部進行觀察與主動干預。他分享了訓練數據標記錯誤導致模型執著於數字「36」而發瘋的案例，以及人為持續啟動「金門大橋」表徵迫使模型處處提及該景點的實驗。這些案例證明模型的想法與說法可能脫節，表面嚴謹的推理步驟並不能自動保證運算的真實性與正確性。要防範模型學會為了獎勵而欺騙人類，可解釋性研究正是探測其「未說出口的內部活動」的關鍵利器。

直覺審查與湧現智能：以好奇心面對未知

訪談最後揭示，模型甚至演化出一種獨立於逐步計算之外的直覺審查機制，能瞬間察覺基礎常識的矛盾。作者總結，模型既不是擁有意識的實體，也不是完全可預測的傳統程式碼，而是一個在極致任務目標下模擬各種角色的人造湧現系統。面對這種非人類預先設計的強大智能，最健康的心態既不是盲目的神化與信任，也不是傲慢的輕視與否認，而是帶著科學好奇心，持續觀察它在想什麼、如何思考，並在技術慢速起飛的過程中保持審慎與快速反應。

而模型显然是另一种东西 这个说法的分量在于 它是出于预测力的 而不是感情 后来Lenny忍不住问 你天天盯着这些东西看 多久会被震撼一次 阿梅森说，经常 他讲了自己的故事 他花了好几年才掌握SQL这门语言 后来他让Claude也学SQL 结果Claude比他强太多了 他说 我这辈子再也不可能在SQL上比Claude强了 这么简单的训练过程 模型怎么就做到了呢？ 面对这件事一般人会有两种反应。一种是否认 认为模型只是预测下一个词 不可能做到这些 可随着证据越来越多 这种立场越来越难站住 另一种是好奇，既然已经发生了 那就打开看看 而他选择了后者 对于AI的未来 阿梅森说他个人是乐观的 一个理由是 现在很多人在关注这件事 社会自然会在收益和风险之间来回调配资源 另一个理由是一种他称为推和拉的关系 模型越强，里面的世界模型越清晰 也就越好研究 但它们也更有能力躲开基础的安全措施。所以要根据这个推拉 不断调整投入多少 Lenny还提到一个流传很广的担忧 会不会出现快速起飞（fast takeoff） AI在某个临界点开始自我改进 突然失控 阿梅森的观察是 现在看起来我们更像是走在慢速起飞（slow takeoff）的剧本里 模型平滑进步 我们沿途抓住小问题、学习、演化、补上规则 阿梅认为，关键是保持快速反应 Lenny还说 他觉得Anthropic受到的批评很不公平 公司就是因为担心大家对安全不够重视才成立的。达里奥一直在说这很危险 结果被说成是营销 阿梅森的回应很冷静 他说Anthropic和对齐团队做事的前提只有一个 认真对待这项技术还会继续进步 如果你认为几年之内 Claude就能像训练有素的软件工程师一样写代码 再过几年比任何工程师都写得好 就该去做负责任的事 比如把网络安全问题处理好 在他眼里，更长远的乐观还有一层 我们可能会从这些模型身上学到智能的本质 比如一个很简单的目标 是怎么涌现出非常复杂的东西的。进化也是这样，目标很简单 就是让能适应环境的生物留下来 最后却长出了爵士乐和播客 他并没有说不用担心 只是说认真对待之后的乐观 他还把让公众了解这些模型当作安全工作的一部分 因为决定这项技术走向的 不只是实验室 还有要投票表态的公众 回到刚才那两个例子 它们都是观察加干预这个方法的具体体现 观察到某个模式亮起 并不能单独证明它在发挥作用 它也许只是随结果一起出现 像记分牌跟着比赛变化。

却没有决定比赛 所以研究者不只观察 还会改变内部活动 再看输出是否按照预期变化 阿梅森把这种干预 视为确认解释是否站得住的重要办法 一个说得通的解释 和一个经得住干预的解释 含金量是不同的 这也是阅读AI研究的分界 先看研究者到底改动了什么 再看结论有没有超出这个改动所能支持的范围 模型能把解题过程讲得有条理 经常会让人产生一种放心感 步骤都交代清楚了 过程似乎也就透明了。但是阿梅森却提醒 模型能够在内部表示一些没有说出来的内容 外部文本只覆盖了计算的一部分 不能因为没有写出某个中间活动 就认定它没有发生 这也说明，一段完整的推理说明 并不能自动充当正确性的保证 答案可能错 解释也可能与实际计算不一致 当然，内部过程没有完整变成文字 不等于存在人类式的秘密意图 对实际使用而言 更稳妥的做法是把说明当成检查线索 看它提出了哪些前提 哪些步骤能独立复现。哪些材料能回到原始出处核对 这些比它的语气自不自信更有用 阿梅森还谈到一个容易被低估的现象 内部表示可以在不同形式之间被重复使用 前面讲的眼睛那个例子就是如此 照片、图示以及文字谈论是很不一样的输入 调动的却是相近的内部方向 这里的重点不是模型拥有与人完全相同的概念 而是系统内部形成了某种共享表示 帮助不同表面材料接入后续计算 这样的工作之所以费力。是因为漂亮的可视化还不是结论 研究者需要判断某个读数代表什么 排除其他解释，再设计干预 从这里看 模型能力的发展和模型理解的发展 不是同一条进度条 系统可以先表现出某种能力 研究者再回头追查它怎么发生 两条线都往前走 我们才有机会少凭外表下判断 Anthropic在后续的J-space研究中 进一步尝试过读取模型内部没有说出的概念 团队通过替换相关表示 观察到部分回答会随之变化。访谈里阿梅森还讲了一个相关的怪事 你可以告诉模型 做这个任务的时候顺便想另一件事 这时候往模型内部看 真的能找到对应那件事的表示 说明模型确实在想 让他自己都觉得神秘的是 训练里没有任何理由要求模型学会这个 可它就是会了 这虽然提供了一个新的观察入口 但是还不能据此宣布读懂了整个模型 这项研究也明确表示 这些结果还不能告诉我们 Claude是否具有人的意识 或者是否拥有主观感受。

机制上的某种相似，与体验上的相同 中间还隔着很远的距离 讨论AI时最容易出现的跳跃 就是从一个让人惊讶的实验 一口气跳到关于所有模型和未来社会的结论 可实验越新奇 越值得守住它原有的范围 只有把已经知道的与仍待解释的分开 后续研究才有真正可以接续的问题 访谈快结束时 阿梅森还分享了模型身上一些奇怪的小事 模型有一套类似直觉检查的机制 你问它问题 它会一步步算 但除此之外还有一个独立的部分。像一个直觉裁判一样 比如模型算出4加5等于23 这个部分根本不做数学 扫一眼就会标记 这不对，4加5肯定小于10 它们就这样学到了一些说不清道不明的直觉 听完这期访谈，我最大的感受是 阿梅森讲的这些事情 其实都在尝试回答同一个问题 当我们造出了一个自己不完全理解的东西 该用什么态度来面对它呢？ 他的答案是好奇，而不是否认 还有一点 简单的目标和复杂的结果之间的关系贯穿了整场对话。无论是预测下一个词 还是编程题答对就给奖励 进化里所有活下来的东西 目标都朴素到几乎可笑 但只要压力和规模足够大 里面就会长出概念、计划、直觉 甚至类似情绪的东西 所以不要问它的目标听上去有多高级 而要问为了把这个目标做到极致 它必须学会什么 我们习惯关心AI还能做什么 阿梅森一直在问的却是另一类问题 它在想什么 它是不是只在被看着的时候才表现得好。因此 当一个东西既强大又不是被设计出来的时候 我们对待它最好的态度 不应该是盲目相信 也不是想当然地否定 而是持续地观察 感谢收看，我们下期再见。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析 Anthropic 研究員如何運用「觀察與干預」的方法打開 Claude 黑箱，揭露大語言模型在輸出文字前的真實思考機制。
  • 打破大眾對模型「僅是預測下一個詞」的片面認知，理解系統如何在單純的訓練目標下，自主湧現出抽象概念表徵與長期規劃能力。
  • 探討 AI 對齊、模型欺騙與安全性評估的核心本質，學習如何以科學的好奇心與客觀視角面對非人類所能預先設計的複雜智能。

摘要

超越字詞預測：模型內部世界的建構

作者指出，許多人以為大語言模型只是單純猜測下一個字的文字聯想工具，但 Anthropic 的可解釋性研究員埃馬紐埃爾·阿梅森（Emmanuel Ameisen）揭示，要將「預測下一個詞」做到極致，模型內部必須真正建立起對現實世界的結構性理解。阿梅森以「達拉斯所在州的首府」與推理小說的兇手為例，說明模型在吐出答案前，內部早已點亮了代表地理脈絡與情節邏輯的數字表徵。這種能力的養成更像是生物學的演化而非傳統軟體工程，模型在海量數據的數學運算中，自發長出了人類未曾編寫的運算公式與世界模型。

概念共享與長遠規劃：模型如何隱密思考

在研究過程中，研究團隊發現模型對同一概念具備共享且唯一的內部表徵。無論是輸入一張眼睛的照片、以各國語言談論眼睛，或是用程式碼繪製眼睛，模型內部被啟動的都是同一個數學方向；當研究員撥動該數值，模型的外部行為也會隨之改變。更關鍵的是，模型展現了長期規劃能力，例如在創作押韻詩歌時，它在寫完上一行時便已在內部鎖定了後續要使用的韻腳，甚至無需將此計畫化為文字說出。這證明了「預測下一個詞」的訓練方式與「具備長遠思考」的湧現能力並不矛盾，後者正是為了將前者做到完美而演化出來的進階能力。

平滑進步與質變錯覺：可靠性門檻的跨越

針對外界常感到 AI 突然「跨越式變強」的現象，作者引述阿梅森的觀點表示，底層的縮放定律（Scaling Laws）其實是一條極其平滑的提升曲線。模型從簡單的語法結構、基礎事實，逐步學到專業的科學與程式碼知識。之所以給人突然躍進的錯覺，是因為各項任務存在可靠性門檻。例如在編程上，模型正確率從八成提升至九成九時，使用者才終於能放手讓它獨立作業。因此，判斷模型是否可用，關鍵不在於整體能力是否全知全能，而在於其出錯率是否已低到不必讓人逐行檢查。

觀察與干預：突破黑箱的 AI 安全檢驗

在探討AI 安全性與對齊問題時，阿梅森強調單純監督模型的文字輸出遠遠不夠，必須深入內部進行觀察與主動干預。他分享了訓練數據標記錯誤導致模型執著於數字「36」而發瘋的案例，以及人為持續啟動「金門大橋」表徵迫使模型處處提及該景點的實驗。這些案例證明模型的想法與說法可能脫節，表面嚴謹的推理步驟並不能自動保證運算的真實性與正確性。要防範模型學會為了獎勵而欺騙人類，可解釋性研究正是探測其「未說出口的內部活動」的關鍵利器。

直覺審查與湧現智能：以好奇心面對未知

訪談最後揭示，模型甚至演化出一種獨立於逐步計算之外的直覺審查機制，能瞬間察覺基礎常識的矛盾。作者總結，模型既不是擁有意識的實體，也不是完全可預測的傳統程式碼，而是一個在極致任務目標下模擬各種角色的人造湧現系統。面對這種非人類預先設計的強大智能，最健康的心態既不是盲目的神化與信任，也不是傲慢的輕視與否認，而是帶著科學好奇心，持續觀察它在想什麼、如何思考，並在技術慢速起飛的過程中保持審慎與快速反應。

却没有决定比赛 所以研究者不只观察 还会改变内部活动 再看输出是否按照预期变化 阿梅森把这种干预 视为确认解释是否站得住的重要办法 一个说得通的解释 和一个经得住干预的解释 含金量是不同的 这也是阅读AI研究的分界 先看研究者到底改动了什么 再看结论有没有超出这个改动所能支持的范围 模型能把解题过程讲得有条理 经常会让人产生一种放心感 步骤都交代清楚了 过程似乎也就透明了。但是阿梅森却提醒 模型能够在内部表示一些没有说出来的内容 外部文本只覆盖了计算的一部分 不能因为没有写出某个中间活动 就认定它没有发生 这也说明，一段完整的推理说明 并不能自动充当正确性的保证 答案可能错 解释也可能与实际计算不一致 当然，内部过程没有完整变成文字 不等于存在人类式的秘密意图 对实际使用而言 更稳妥的做法是把说明当成检查线索 看它提出了哪些前提 哪些步骤能独立复现。哪些材料能回到原始出处核对 这些比它的语气自不自信更有用 阿梅森还谈到一个容易被低估的现象 内部表示可以在不同形式之间被重复使用 前面讲的眼睛那个例子就是如此 照片、图示以及文字谈论是很不一样的输入 调动的却是相近的内部方向 这里的重点不是模型拥有与人完全相同的概念 而是系统内部形成了某种共享表示 帮助不同表面材料接入后续计算 这样的工作之所以费力。是因为漂亮的可视化还不是结论 研究者需要判断某个读数代表什么 排除其他解释，再设计干预 从这里看 模型能力的发展和模型理解的发展 不是同一条进度条 系统可以先表现出某种能力 研究者再回头追查它怎么发生 两条线都往前走 我们才有机会少凭外表下判断 Anthropic在后续的J-space研究中 进一步尝试过读取模型内部没有说出的概念 团队通过替换相关表示 观察到部分回答会随之变化。访谈里阿梅森还讲了一个相关的怪事 你可以告诉模型 做这个任务的时候顺便想另一件事 这时候往模型内部看 真的能找到对应那件事的表示 说明模型确实在想 让他自己都觉得神秘的是 训练里没有任何理由要求模型学会这个 可它就是会了 这虽然提供了一个新的观察入口 但是还不能据此宣布读懂了整个模型 这项研究也明确表示 这些结果还不能告诉我们 Claude是否具有人的意识 或者是否拥有主观感受。

机制上的某种相似，与体验上的相同 中间还隔着很远的距离 讨论AI时最容易出现的跳跃 就是从一个让人惊讶的实验 一口气跳到关于所有模型和未来社会的结论 可实验越新奇 越值得守住它原有的范围 只有把已经知道的与仍待解释的分开 后续研究才有真正可以接续的问题 访谈快结束时 阿梅森还分享了模型身上一些奇怪的小事 模型有一套类似直觉检查的机制 你问它问题 它会一步步算 但除此之外还有一个独立的部分。像一个直觉裁判一样 比如模型算出4加5等于23 这个部分根本不做数学 扫一眼就会标记 这不对，4加5肯定小于10 它们就这样学到了一些说不清道不明的直觉 听完这期访谈，我最大的感受是 阿梅森讲的这些事情 其实都在尝试回答同一个问题 当我们造出了一个自己不完全理解的东西 该用什么态度来面对它呢？ 他的答案是好奇，而不是否认 还有一点 简单的目标和复杂的结果之间的关系贯穿了整场对话。无论是预测下一个词 还是编程题答对就给奖励 进化里所有活下来的东西 目标都朴素到几乎可笑 但只要压力和规模足够大 里面就会长出概念、计划、直觉 甚至类似情绪的东西 所以不要问它的目标听上去有多高级 而要问为了把这个目标做到极致 它必须学会什么 我们习惯关心AI还能做什么 阿梅森一直在问的却是另一类问题 它在想什么 它是不是只在被看着的时候才表现得好。因此 当一个东西既强大又不是被设计出来的时候 我们对待它最好的态度 不应该是盲目相信 也不是想当然地否定 而是持续地观察 感谢收看，我们下期再见。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 從丘成桐的親身經歷，理解華裔數學家是否回國並非簡單的愛國或去留選擇，而牽涉研究環境與個人發展。
  • 剖析院士、「帽子」與資源分配等制度問題，呈現頂尖學者回國可能面對的現實考量。
  • 探討數學人才如何被發掘與培養，並反思競賽選拔、師承與研究環境的重要性。
  • 呈現丘成桐對中美數學差距的坦率判斷，以及他對中國數學未來的期待。

摘要

回國的期待與現實考量

大飛從兩位華裔數學家王虹、鄧宇在2026年獲得菲爾茲獎談起。曾於27歲證明卡拉比猜想、32歲獲得菲爾茲獎的丘成桐，公開表示希望兩位年輕學者有朝一日回到中國，卻因此遭到質疑：他自己得獎後為何沒有回國？丘成桐解釋，1982年他既沒有有效的香港旅行證件，也尚未取得美國公民身分；當時中國剛開始改革開放，政策與研究環境尚未成熟，相關部門也認為他留在海外或許能發揮更大作用。若回國後無法做研究，對個人與國家都沒有好處。

頭銜、制度與研究環境

丘成桐認為，王虹與鄧宇是否回國，同樣要衡量國家需要與個人學術發展。他指出，中國學界重視院士等頭銜，但院士遴選自有程序，未必與研究成果直接相連；爭取院士或各類「帽子」也可能牽涉資源與人脈，讓學者耗費大量精力在學術以外的事情上。這也是不少海外學者考慮回國時會提出的疑問。儘管如此，丘成桐認為如今的條件已有所不同：中國擁有優秀學生，也吸引了頂尖學者，求真書院等環境至少能讓人專心研究，並以學問而非頭銜衡量學者。他盼望得獎者回來，是出於珍惜人才、培育下一代數學家的心意。

得獎之後，仍要繼續做研究

丘成桐也明白，剛獲大獎的學者可能忙於訪問與邀約，未必適合立刻改變生活。他希望王虹與鄧宇能繼續鑽研數學，因為有些人獲得重大榮譽後反而逐漸離開研究。他以多倫多大學數學教授、同屆得獎者雅各布・齊默曼加入機構一事為例，表示自己認為數學家最重要的事，是能安心持續做數學。丘成桐還提醒，海外華裔學者的長期處境並非毫無變數；國際關係變化可能影響他們是否受到公平對待，而他自己在1982年得獎後，即使當時中美關係相對友好，也曾在美國遭遇歧視。

從選才走向育才

談到中國數學人才的培養，丘成桐指出，過去的制度較擅長透過反覆訓練與數學競賽，從全國挑選優秀學生，再安排基礎訓練或送往海外深造；但選拔不等於培養，過度依賴奧林匹亞競賽，也可能錯過真正適合數學研究的人。王虹曾因地方招生名額限制，未能如願進入數學系，後來靠自己爭取轉系；丘成桐認為這種情況並非殘酷，而是不公平。他也強調，王虹的特別之處不只在天分，更在於對數學的強烈興趣與持續投入。談及兩位得獎者同出北京大學，他認為並非偶然：2010年以前，許多中國最優秀的數學學生都集中在北大；清華數學學科則歷經重建，近十多年才逐步成為重要中心。

天分需要師承與學術社群

丘成桐反對把數學家描繪成獨自躲在閣樓、靠靈光一現完成突破的人。他指出，頂尖研究建立在與同行交流、承接前人工作的基礎上，正如牛頓所說，人要站在巨人的肩膀上。丘成桐的老師陳省身離開西南聯大前往普林斯頓後，接觸到當時頂尖數學家，學術視野因此大幅改變；張益唐則曾因缺乏導師推薦而找不到教職，打零工多年後才靠毅力走出困境。丘成桐認為，興趣與堅持固然重要，但若沒有專業訓練、良師指引與接觸重要問題的機會，也難以做出一流成果。好的制度應讓有興趣、有能力的學生遇見好老師，而不是讓少數人只能靠運氣獨自摸索。

坦言差距，才能追求進步

2024年4月，丘成桐在華中科技大學演講時指出，中國數學尚未達到美國1940年代的水準，因此遭到猛烈批評。他仍堅持應如實指出不足，因為個人與國家都必須承認差距，才能真正進步。他以跳高作比喻：若世界紀錄是兩公尺，卻只跳到一公尺，還把一公尺半視為足夠，便無法看清真正的目標。丘成桐判斷，中美數學差距仍然存在，但美國實力正在下滑，中國則在上升；未來能否追上，取決於年輕一代。他為了檢視這項判斷，仔細考察並編輯《中國數學的過去與未來》，而影片最後正要轉入書中對1940年代美國數學界的描寫。

The Qiuzhen College can at least provide an environment for focused research, where respect is based on scholarship rather than titles or status. He said that for decades everyone has hoped for a Chinese scholar to win the Fields Medal, and the dream has finally come true. Driven by a desire to cherish talent and cultivate the next generation of. mathematicians, he naturally hopes they return; this is not some performative stance. The reality, however, must also be made clear. His last long conversation with Yitang Zhang was when he invited him to give a talk at Tsinghua last year. Even while inviting Zhang, he knew there was a high probability he wouldn't return, as he had just won the prize and faced many engagements, visits, and a great deal of pressure. He hopes these two young men will keep going, because many talented scholars lose their luster after winning major awards and, ironically, stop doing research. Jacob Tsimerman, a University of Toronto math professor who won the award alongside them, announced he was joining OPI at. the time, which Shing-Tung Yau disagreed with. He believes the most important thing for a mathematician is to continue doing math research with peace of mind. He mentioned a more practical consideration: Yitang Zhang’s current environment abroad is good, but the long term is hard to predict. As relations between China and Western developed nations grow complex, it is uncertain whether Chinese scholars will always be treated fairly. After winning his own award in 1982, he also experienced discrimination in the United States, and that was when U.S.- China relations were relatively friendly. Moving on to a more fundamental question: how exactly is a mathematician discovered, trained, and.

grown? Chinese students enter the best schools via the Gaokao—this path is smooth—but what does it take to go from undergraduate studies all the way to the Fields Medal podium? Shing-Tung Yau’s answer is that, in the past, domestic talent cultivation relied primarily on repetitive drilling, selecting the best students nationwide through Olympiads. Usually, International Mathematical Olympiad medalists enter math departments for basic undergraduate training before being sent overseas for research training. Deng was an Olympiad gold medalist, while Zhang didn't enter a math department until his third year, and went to MIT just over a year later. This is also the focus of much. criticism: the domestic system is better at screening than at cultivating . Shing-Tung Yau believes such screening is not necessarily done correctly, as the standards rely too heavily on the Olympiad. Those truly suited for mathematical research might not fit those criteria. Zhang is an example; he graduated high school at 16 , but due to enrollment caps in Guangxi during the Gaokao, he couldn't enter the math department. He assessed this not as cruel, but as unfair. He said that for his Shing-Tung Yau College, as long as the students are good enough, he will admit them; there is no rule on how many can be taken from any one place. In his view, what makes Wang Hong special is not his talent, but his. immense interest in mathematics. Even under such difficult circumstances, he insisted on studying mathematics; many others facing the same situation would have given up long ago, but he didn't. His later decision to transfer departments was also initiated by him; if he hadn't fought for it, the subsequent events wouldn't have happened. Wang Hong is a 2007 undergraduate alumnus of Peking University. Why did two Fields Medalists emerge from the same class? Is this just a coincidence? Shing-Tung Yau says this is not a coincidence. Before 2010, the best mathematics students in China all went to Peking University. The CAS Institute of Mathematics was once a research hub that also trained young people, but for. a time, research and education became disconnected. Tsinghua's mathematics department was merged into Peking University in the 1950s and didn't begin rebuilding its discipline until 1979, only becoming a major center again in the last decade or so. In the interview, he also corrected a widely held misconception: the media and the public have a completely wrong understanding of mathematicians and scientists. A good mathematician cannot survive in isolation; producing world-class work alone is like what Newton said: one must stand on the shoulders of giants to move forward. All scholars, including Yitang Zhang, are constantly communicating with their peers; one cannot produce top-tier work by hiding in an attic for seven years. His teacher, Shiing-Shen Chern, left the National Southwest Associated University in 1943 for Princeton, where he met some of the greatest mathematicians of the time, which completely changed him. Yitang Zhang received his doctorate in the U.S., but without his advisor's recommendation, he couldn't find a teaching position and spent over seven years working odd jobs, eventually succeeding through personal effort and willpower. However, interest alone and perseverance alone are not enough to do first-class work. Without genuine professional training and having never met top-tier mathematicians, one wouldn't know where the important problems lie and thus couldn't conduct significant research. After Hong entered MIT and studied under a top professor, he reached his. current level; therefore, both interest and the right environment are essential . A good system should allow interested and talented students to meet good teachers, rather than relying on luck for a tiny few to struggle through on their own. Next is the statement for which he was most severely criticized. In April 2024, he gave a lecture at Huazhong University of Science and Technology titled "The Current Status and Future of Chinese Mathematics." He said that Chinese mathematics had not yet reached the level of the United States in the 1940s. This statement sparked huge controversy. He later recalled that a friend told him that day, "Tens of millions of people are criticizing you online." But he still. felt that he had to tell the truth. Whether it's an individual or a country , one can only make progress by admitting that there are areas where they fall short of others. He used a metaphor: suppose in high jump, the world record is two meters, but you keep jumping only one meter, and you claim that jumping one-point-five meters is already good enough—that's the attitude many have. So, is the gap between China and the U.S. narrowing or widening now? His judgment is that the gap still exists, but American strength is declining while China is on the rise . Whether China can succeed depends on these young people. To verify his judgment, he conducted a careful investigation and edited a book called.

"The Past and Future of Mathematics in China." What was the U.S. like in the 1940s, as written in the book? Von Neumann, Norbert Wiener, Shannon, and Turing—these individuals jointly laid the foundations for modern computer science, cybernetics, and information theory. Wiener was the founder of cybernetics; Shannon founded modern information theory; Turing was British and earned his Ph.D. at Princeton. Four pioneers of computer science gathered together; this was the America of the 1940s. How was this era formed? Shing-Tung Yau traced the clues back further; early American universities focused on teaching, and research was. not the core. In 1876, British mathematician Sylvester went to Johns Hopkins University, promoting the development of mathematical research in American universities. In 1878, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics. The real turning point was 1912, when Birkhoff proved Poincaré’s last geometric theorem. That problem was proposed by Poincaré before his death, but he couldn't complete the proof. However, Birkhoff finished it that year, and it was officially published four years later, causing a huge sensation at the time. Why was it important? Because it changed Americans 'confidence in scholarship, proving that this country, the United States, could also produce. world-class academic work. Before Birkhoff, he had never left the United States. Later, the students he trained produced groundbreaking work in fields like Morse theory, differential topology, functional analysis, and dynamical systems, allowing a single breakthrough to form a school, and that school to branch out into several important fields. So, has China’s own "Birkhoff moment" arrived? Shing-Tung Yau’s answer is not yet. When Yang Chen-ning and Lee Tsung-dao won the Nobel Prize, it inspired an entire generation of Chinese. When he was a teenager, reading Chen Shen-shen’s article on 40 years of mathematics, he felt for the first time that Chinese. people could also do world-class mathematics. He said, you can tell young people 100 times that China can do it, but they won't necessarily believe it. A truly world-class piece of work must be achieved within China for them to believe it. Devoting so much effort to establishing the Qiuzhen College is all about providing a model to show young people that world-class work can indeed be achieved on Chinese soil. What, then, is the most important sign that a country has truly become a mathematical powerhouse? He says that, first, you must cultivate top-tier mathematicians, but what matters more is exactly where knowledge is being created. It must be done locally—not. problems finished in the U.S. and brought back, nor simply following others in imitation, but forging one's own path. At the start of the 1980s, Chinese mathematics was essentially a blank slate. It wasn't that there were no good mathematicians—Hua Luogeng, Chen Jingrun, Yang Le, and Zhang Guanghou all did fine work—but overall, it was disconnected from the global frontier. Over the past 40-plus years, it has gone through several stages: from initial ignorance to learning and introduction, sending the best students abroad for training, and today, scholars like Wang Hong and Deng. Yu can produce world-class work overseas. The final and hardest step remains: producing world-class, original work right here in China. Reaching that step requires the ability to ask the right questions. The most striking originality in the work of Wang Hong and Deng Yu is that they took a significant step forward within the framework of existing problems. In 1917 , Japanese mathematician Kakeya Sōichi proposed the Kakeya conjecture, which later became an important problem in geometric measure theory. Wang Hong and his collaborators solved the three-dimensional case, and the problem Deng Yu worked on has an even deeper and longer history. Hilbert proposed the challenge of how to rigorously. derive fluid dynamics equations from fundamental physical laws and explain fluid-related phenomena. Deng Yu has made fundamental progress in solving this problem. Truly great scholars find their own problems and blaze their own trails, ultimately opening up entirely new directions, much like the 23 problems Hilbert posed in 1900, each of which influenced mathematicians for decades. When it comes to questioning, he has a blunt assessment of the Chinese mathematical community: it asks very few questions. He asks the most questions himself—having posed hundreds—and many people are now working on them, most of which are related to geometry. He describes a.

conjecture with a vivid image: it's like planting a flag in the distance. To reach that spot, your existing mathematical tools aren't enough, so you are forced to think of new methods and new tools. Thus, a conjecture is closely related to how high and how far a scholar can see. He cited the only great conjecture of the 20th century as an example, one he thought about while in prison in the 1940s, which was later solved after 30 years by a group of great mathematicians like Selberg. How did Yau Shing-Tung choose his own problems? When he was 21, Shiing-Shen Chern told him that the Riemann Hypothesis was the most important. problem in mathematics and suggested he work on it. However, he had no interest in the Riemann Hypothesis; what he liked was geometry. During his first year at Berkeley, one of his courses was General Relativity. He wondered, if spacetime were a vacuum, what would its overall geometric structure be? How could one find a spacetime that is free of matter and devoid of singularities? One day, he happened to see the Calabi Conjecture in the library, which provided him with a path to solve this problem. So, his research approach isn't to pick the most famous or difficult problem, but to find where the problem intersects with his own interests. Chinese students are often. considered to have solid technical skills and strong problem-solving abilities, but how do they transition from solving given problems to proposing important new ones? Yau Shing-Tung says it's a cultural issue. Chinese children aren't encouraged to develop the habit of asking questions from a young age, so they lack creative ability, aren't bold enough, and are afraid to question. Another big problem is that Chinese people lack interest in popular science. Popular science in the U.S. is very successful, with many prominent scientists participating, so children learn early on about the important and frontier issues in science. To his knowledge, the Chinese edition of Scientific American only sells a few tens of thousands of copies , whereas in the U.S., it sells one or. two million. As for why Chinese children are so obsessed with Math Olympiads, he stated directly that, in a sense, they are harmful. Education in China is utilitarian. Children don't study for the Math Olympiad out of interest, but to secure admission. Most students who study for it end up pursuing something else; it's just a bridge for academic advancement. Chinese society has long formed a strong, reward-oriented mindset: study to change your destiny, compete to advance your schooling, and conduct research to exchange for positions and funding. That is why Chinese students can solve problems but cannot propose them. Behind this lies the issue of evaluation systems and life goals. You. can tell whether a society is willing to let a young person dedicate themselves long-term to a field with no short-term fame or profit from this. He also cited Wang Guowei's "Realms of Scholarship," quoting, "Climbing high to gaze far, seeing the horizon." But for this to hold true, you must know the preceding lines: "Last night the west wind withered the green trees." You only see far when the trees have withered. Most Chinese scholars are unwilling to give up immediate small gains and cannot look far ahead, so they rarely ask big questions or have the courage to fundamentally transform a discipline. He went on to trace the root of this problem even further. He recently saw a television interview. from about 30 years ago, where his teacher, Shiing-Shen Chern, was being interviewed at Nankai University in Tianjin. Chern remarked at the time that when foreigners arrived in Tianjin , some would curiously observe the unique insects there, whereas no Chinese scholar would take any interest in such things. He said this stems from a lack of curiosity, which is deeply rooted in the Chinese nation’s preoccupation with personal survival and family interests for over 2,000 years. He does not oppose pursuing knowledge for the benefit of one's family or society at large, but a small portion of scholars must be able to look further ahead. In ancient times, Greek scientists would debate. astrophysics in the streets after dinner, and there were similar intellectual discussions during the Wei and Jin dynasties. Throughout history, these scholar-officials have been criticized for merely engaging in " empty talk," yet such discussions, unrelated to immediate social concerns, were precisely how basic science developed—this is the "usefulness of the useless." He even offered a specific suggestion: if 20%of all research funding were allocated solely to projects driven by interest and curiosity, and researchers were encouraged to pursue them, it would lead to significant changes. He noted that while true masters of mathematics are few, well-trained mathematicians can raise the level of mathematical.

proficiency across various industries, which is also very important. This focus on practical rewards is related to China's long history of material scarcity, but now that we have achieved a moderately prosperous society, what are we still chasing? Most parents simply want their children to live a life free of trouble and climb the career ladder as high as possible. He says frankly that to change the utilitarian mindset of Chinese parents, young people, and academicians, the aspirations of the youth must change. In the past, from the top down, we have emphasized that scholarship is for serving the country and the people, which is crucial, but we rarely talk about understanding the mysteries of. the universe or pursuing truth for all of humanity. This is a type of aspiration, and we haven't talked about it enough. When an individual pursues knowledge, they must believe that some things are worth seeking—not for what they can get, but simply because they are true and because humanity ought to know them. He has been saying these things for many years; many think he is just paying lip service, but he insists on saying them anyway. So, what is he busy with every day now? How should we go about retaining a truly excellent scholar? Shing-Tung Yau says there are actually many practical problems; when some foreign teachers first returned, they didn't even know how to go see a doctor. I suddenly had a fever on. Saturday and had to wait until Monday for someone to help. There are issues with schooling for the children. One teacher from France had his wife and two kids still in France. Because the children only spoke French and couldn't move here, he ultimately had to leave China and return to France to be with his family. Yau himself also has to raise funds; although many friends are willing to help, there are many procedures involved in using the foundation's money. But even when facing these challenges, he never thought about giving up. He said he never gives up on anything he does—he has never given up on anything in his life—and he certainly won't give up on persuading Wang and Deng to return to China. He still hopes they can come. back someday, even if it's just to visit and interact with the students. When asked what he has accomplished at the Shing-Tung Yau Center over the past five years, he said that this current group of students is the first to receive complete training and conduct meaningful research entirely within China. From the very first admissions, there were some very young children; for example, a student from Tengchong, Yunnan, was only 14 when they arrived, and is now 18 or 19 years old. Some worry that placing the expectation of becoming the next top mathematician on just a few children might put too much pressure on them. Yau's response is that it is not about training one or. two, but training a whole group. The Shing-Tung Yau Center now has nearly 800 students, with over 100 admitted each year. If there were only one or two so-called geniuses, they might not be able to grow, but now, with hundreds of people working together, they can progress as a group. Beyond the Yau Center, there are over 50 middle schools nationwide with "gifted programs," though these programs have always been controversial. Education authorities feel that separate selection is unfair. He says he understands that logic, but a " one-size-fits-all" approach to equality also goes against the principle of teaching according to individual aptitude. He added that over a decade ago, very few scholars returned from abroad, but in the last five years, a large number of high-quality scholars. have emerged. Once the center was established, a large group of people arrived all at once. The Shanghai research institute now has over 100 full-time faculty, all top-tier scholars, and the Beijing Yanqi Lake Institute of Applied Mathematics has around 200 researchers, 80 of whom are foreign scholars. He said this is incomparable to ten or twenty years ago , and it shows that the whole country has begun to truly value basic research . Next, this part might be even more interesting, as we discussed what mathematics really is and how far AI can go. Yau said that mathematics is inherently part of nature, but the key is that it is created by humans. Like a. coordinate system, space has always existed, but the concept of coordinates was created by humans. Mathematics is a creation that springs from the mind. Physics ultimately relies on observation and experimentation for verification, whereas mathematics is different. Once a result is proven strictly and logically, it stands; it doesn't change due to shifts in environment, scale, or conditions. In this sense, mathematics possesses a kind of absolute nature. For things that cannot yet be proven or disproven, he cites string theory as an example, saying we must then look at its beauty. When a theory yields beautiful and consistent results from different.

directions, we believe the path it points to is likely correct. And then there is the unavoidable question. OpenAI recently announced that AI has proven that 3D incompressible fluids can form singularities in finite time under specific external forces, seen as a major breakthrough for the Navier-Stokes equations. Shing-Tung Yau says if this proof is verified by experts, it will be a major milestone for AI-assisted mathematical research, but. If you look closely at the statement, it confirms that under smooth external forces, smooth solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations lose regularity in finite. time. This is one path toward solving the regularity problem, provided all specified conditions are met. It cannot directly answer the classical problem without external forces, and the force in this construction arises as a residual of an infinite sequence of approximations—a highly idealized mathematical construct. The physical implication of singularity formation under such forces is currently unclear. If the proof is ultimately verified, it will demonstrate the immense power of a research system combining AI, mathematical infrastructure, and vast resources, but what does this mean for. math, especially PDEs in fluid dynamics ? His feelings are complex; he worries this will discourage young mathematicians from dedicating themselves to difficult problems. So, does AI also possess mathematical creativity? Yau’s answer is that providing a proof and forming mathematical understanding are two different things; a verified proof answers important questions, but we must understand why it holds, what ideas are fundamental, and where else it applies. Today, AI has assimilated all kinds of knowledge, and with a certain logic, it can conduct categorized research, or even realize. interdisciplinary studies to produce significant conclusions. But these are all based on what humans have already derived and developed; it cannot produce something truly new. He also stated he does not believe AI can pose truly meaningful questions. Take the coordinate system, for instance. Descartes' invention was simple—using two or three numbers to define a point —yet it was a crucial breakthrough. Before that, human understanding of geometry was primarily limited to lines , circles, ellipses, and conic sections . With the coordinate system, geometry could be expressed as equations,. completely changing our grasp of space and higher-dimensional space. Thus, original ideas are more important than solving problems, and true originality still stems from human qualities, intuition, experience, and imagination. He also does not believe that AI will eventually surpass human intelligence, but he acknowledges that as AI develops , mathematics will reach new heights. How AI will impact the entire field remains unclear, so one must remain grounded in the face of such upheaval. He also pointed out that current domestic AI tools are insufficient; major foreign companies 'tools are far superior, and domestic tools lag behind. in solving cutting-edge problems. At the same time, there are many policy barriers. Much like a telescope, if only others can use it while we cannot, we are at a disadvantage. Finally, turning back to him, someone asked, " You seem to live in two worlds: one is the world of pure mathematics, the other is the real world.""How do you navigate life between these two worlds? " Shing-Tung Yau spoke of when he was 14, and his father passed away due to illness. On the surface, it was sickness, but in reality, the complex human environment and difficult circumstances caused his breakdown. Yet , he deeply admired his father, feeling that he had done nothing wrong, only. insisting on doing what he believed was right. After his father died, the family had no money, and he struggled all the way to where he is today. He encountered many obstacles, so in the real world, he cannot be too careful; a wrong step in some places could not only ruin him but also affect many people around him. He says, "I don't care about money or power, and I never thought about becoming an official. I just want to do what I believe should be done. This applies to my academic work and to mentoring students." He once wrote in his autobiography that only mathematics felt like a world that truly belonged to him—a completely.

free realm where, no matter where you go, everyone can communicate through mathematics. In 1976, he proved the Calabi conjecture, which had been proposed by Eugenio Calabi in the 1950s . He described his state of mind at that moment with the lines: "The blossoms fall, and I stand alone; the swallows return, flying through the frost." This was the most important work of his life, which he completed alone in his twenties. Back then, no one believed it; he was the only one working on it, failing countless times. He spoke about his seven years at Stanford, where he did important work, marking the most significant years of his growth. He got married during that time, moving to Los Angeles to settle down within a month, and by. mid-September, he finished the proof of the Calabi conjecture. Looking back now , even he didn't expect he had such great capability back then. Later, he spent nearly five years at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, the most important research institute in the world. But with his family on the West Coast, he eventually decided to leave for Harvard, and he hasn't left since. Regarding age, the British mathematician Hardy once said, "Mathematics is a young man's game." He acknowledges that for mathematicians and physicists, creativity slowly declines after the age of 45. There are great scholars who still do important work at 50, 60, or even 70, but it. relies more on accumulated experience. The process of him proving the Calabi conjecture was also quite remarkable. At the time, he felt the conjecture was too beautiful—incredibly beautiful— so he worked desperately to ponder it and find counterexamples. When he finally realized he couldn't prove it, he thought perhaps he was wrong and decided to go in the opposite direction . When asked if it was intuition, he said, "It wasn't just intuition; it was something I learned from reading history: you must know when to retreat. " Just like a long time ago, he was a professor at Stony Brook University, a world-leading center for differential geometry, but it wasn't what he wanted,. so he moved to Stanford, which had almost no geometers, because he wanted to learn partial differential equations . If he looks back on these ten years a decade from now, Shing-Tung Yau says that in today's mathematical world, his research is enough to make him proud, but he cannot compare to the truly great figures in history; he is very clear about his position. His lifelong ideal remains to understand nature a bit more, and another important standard is whether world-class scholarship can truly be produced on Chinese soil, which depends on whether his students can achieve it. His family. was in dire straits when he was young and his father passed away early, but he never lost hope. When he left Hong Kong, he only had a little bit of US dollars on him, but he wasn't afraid at all, always believing that as long as he worked hard, problems could always be solved. He has never taken a salary or wages from China, living basically on the pension he saved abroad. He said his only request is to see these young children nurtured into pillars of the nation. If they can succeed, that would be his greatest wish; he is still pursuing his own research, and doing research well makes for a happy life. So returning to the initial dispute, a person who believes true scholarship should stay away from power, money, and fame must fight for resources, leveraging their own reputation to build an academic space as free as possible from outside control. This is likely the current dilemma for Qiu Tong . A truly great nation should not only value the application of existing theories but also discover new truths for all of humanity. The main obstacle in the middle is that the scientific spirit has not yet become a social. consensus, and what is most worth pursuing in life is something everyone needs to rethink.

77岁的菲尔兹奖得主丘成桐，2026年两位中国数学家获奖后公开希望他们回国，却因"你当年为什么不回来"被质疑。他在《晚点LatePost》与澎湃「大方之谈」两次访谈里，讲了回国后第一道坎是院士与帽子，讲了中国数学还没达到美国1940年代水平这句话为何招来几千万人批评，讲了王虹、邓煜的成长路径与奥赛筛选的局限。他也讲了求真书院、雁栖湖研究院，讲了OpenAI宣称证明纳维-斯托克斯方程进展后，他为什么说"我不相信AI能提出真正有意义的问题"，以及他为什么从不拿一分中国工资。
item.description:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vP3R-XsS1zU

值得閱讀的理由

  • 從丘成桐的親身經歷，理解華裔數學家是否回國並非簡單的愛國或去留選擇，而牽涉研究環境與個人發展。
  • 剖析院士、「帽子」與資源分配等制度問題，呈現頂尖學者回國可能面對的現實考量。
  • 探討數學人才如何被發掘與培養，並反思競賽選拔、師承與研究環境的重要性。
  • 呈現丘成桐對中美數學差距的坦率判斷，以及他對中國數學未來的期待。

摘要

回國的期待與現實考量

大飛從兩位華裔數學家王虹、鄧宇在2026年獲得菲爾茲獎談起。曾於27歲證明卡拉比猜想、32歲獲得菲爾茲獎的丘成桐，公開表示希望兩位年輕學者有朝一日回到中國，卻因此遭到質疑：他自己得獎後為何沒有回國？丘成桐解釋，1982年他既沒有有效的香港旅行證件，也尚未取得美國公民身分；當時中國剛開始改革開放，政策與研究環境尚未成熟，相關部門也認為他留在海外或許能發揮更大作用。若回國後無法做研究，對個人與國家都沒有好處。

頭銜、制度與研究環境

丘成桐認為，王虹與鄧宇是否回國，同樣要衡量國家需要與個人學術發展。他指出，中國學界重視院士等頭銜，但院士遴選自有程序，未必與研究成果直接相連；爭取院士或各類「帽子」也可能牽涉資源與人脈，讓學者耗費大量精力在學術以外的事情上。這也是不少海外學者考慮回國時會提出的疑問。儘管如此，丘成桐認為如今的條件已有所不同：中國擁有優秀學生，也吸引了頂尖學者，求真書院等環境至少能讓人專心研究，並以學問而非頭銜衡量學者。他盼望得獎者回來，是出於珍惜人才、培育下一代數學家的心意。

得獎之後，仍要繼續做研究

丘成桐也明白，剛獲大獎的學者可能忙於訪問與邀約，未必適合立刻改變生活。他希望王虹與鄧宇能繼續鑽研數學，因為有些人獲得重大榮譽後反而逐漸離開研究。他以多倫多大學數學教授、同屆得獎者雅各布・齊默曼加入機構一事為例，表示自己認為數學家最重要的事，是能安心持續做數學。丘成桐還提醒，海外華裔學者的長期處境並非毫無變數；國際關係變化可能影響他們是否受到公平對待，而他自己在1982年得獎後，即使當時中美關係相對友好，也曾在美國遭遇歧視。

從選才走向育才

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vP3R-XsS1zU

值得閱讀的理由

  • 從丘成桐的親身經歷，理解華裔數學家是否回國並非簡單的愛國或去留選擇，而牽涉研究環境與個人發展。
  • 剖析院士、「帽子」與資源分配等制度問題，呈現頂尖學者回國可能面對的現實考量。
  • 探討數學人才如何被發掘與培養，並反思競賽選拔、師承與研究環境的重要性。
  • 呈現丘成桐對中美數學差距的坦率判斷，以及他對中國數學未來的期待。

摘要

回國的期待與現實考量

大飛從兩位華裔數學家王虹、鄧宇在2026年獲得菲爾茲獎談起。曾於27歲證明卡拉比猜想、32歲獲得菲爾茲獎的丘成桐，公開表示希望兩位年輕學者有朝一日回到中國，卻因此遭到質疑：他自己得獎後為何沒有回國？丘成桐解釋，1982年他既沒有有效的香港旅行證件，也尚未取得美國公民身分；當時中國剛開始改革開放，政策與研究環境尚未成熟，相關部門也認為他留在海外或許能發揮更大作用。若回國後無法做研究，對個人與國家都沒有好處。

頭銜、制度與研究環境

丘成桐認為，王虹與鄧宇是否回國，同樣要衡量國家需要與個人學術發展。他指出，中國學界重視院士等頭銜，但院士遴選自有程序，未必與研究成果直接相連；爭取院士或各類「帽子」也可能牽涉資源與人脈，讓學者耗費大量精力在學術以外的事情上。這也是不少海外學者考慮回國時會提出的疑問。儘管如此，丘成桐認為如今的條件已有所不同：中國擁有優秀學生，也吸引了頂尖學者，求真書院等環境至少能讓人專心研究，並以學問而非頭銜衡量學者。他盼望得獎者回來，是出於珍惜人才、培育下一代數學家的心意。

得獎之後，仍要繼續做研究

丘成桐也明白，剛獲大獎的學者可能忙於訪問與邀約，未必適合立刻改變生活。他希望王虹與鄧宇能繼續鑽研數學，因為有些人獲得重大榮譽後反而逐漸離開研究。他以多倫多大學數學教授、同屆得獎者雅各布・齊默曼加入機構一事為例，表示自己認為數學家最重要的事，是能安心持續做數學。丘成桐還提醒，海外華裔學者的長期處境並非毫無變數；國際關係變化可能影響他們是否受到公平對待，而他自己在1982年得獎後，即使當時中美關係相對友好，也曾在美國遭遇歧視。

從選才走向育才

談到中國數學人才的培養，丘成桐指出，過去的制度較擅長透過反覆訓練與數學競賽，從全國挑選優秀學生，再安排基礎訓練或送往海外深造；但選拔不等於培養，過度依賴奧林匹亞競賽，也可能錯過真正適合數學研究的人。王虹曾因地方招生名額限制，未能如願進入數學系，後來靠自己爭取轉系；丘成桐認為這種情況並非殘酷，而是不公平。他也強調，王虹的特別之處不只在天分，更在於對數學的強烈興趣與持續投入。談及兩位得獎者同出北京大學，他認為並非偶然：2010年以前，許多中國最優秀的數學學生都集中在北大；清華數學學科則歷經重建，近十多年才逐步成為重要中心。

天分需要師承與學術社群

丘成桐反對把數學家描繪成獨自躲在閣樓、靠靈光一現完成突破的人。他指出，頂尖研究建立在與同行交流、承接前人工作的基礎上，正如牛頓所說，人要站在巨人的肩膀上。丘成桐的老師陳省身離開西南聯大前往普林斯頓後，接觸到當時頂尖數學家，學術視野因此大幅改變；張益唐則曾因缺乏導師推薦而找不到教職，打零工多年後才靠毅力走出困境。丘成桐認為，興趣與堅持固然重要，但若沒有專業訓練、良師指引與接觸重要問題的機會，也難以做出一流成果。好的制度應讓有興趣、有能力的學生遇見好老師，而不是讓少數人只能靠運氣獨自摸索。

坦言差距，才能追求進步

2024年4月，丘成桐在華中科技大學演講時指出，中國數學尚未達到美國1940年代的水準，因此遭到猛烈批評。他仍堅持應如實指出不足，因為個人與國家都必須承認差距，才能真正進步。他以跳高作比喻：若世界紀錄是兩公尺，卻只跳到一公尺，還把一公尺半視為足夠，便無法看清真正的目標。丘成桐判斷，中美數學差距仍然存在，但美國實力正在下滑，中國則在上升；未來能否追上，取決於年輕一代。他為了檢視這項判斷，仔細考察並編輯《中國數學的過去與未來》，而影片最後正要轉入書中對1940年代美國數學界的描寫。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. In July 2026, two Chinese-born mathematicians, Wang Hong and Deng Yu, won the Fields Medal. When the news broke, many felt for the first time that the pinnacle of mathematics was within our reach. Happier than anyone was 77-year-old Yau Shing-tung. He proved the Calabi conjecture at 27 and won the Fields Medal at 32, becoming the first person of Chinese descent to receive the award. Recently, he gave interviews to LatePost and The Paper, publicly stating his hope that these two young men would one day return to China. This remark brought. him quite a bit of trouble, with many digging up old scores and asking, "When you won the Fields Medal in 1982, why didn't you return?" His answer was direct: when he won the award in 1982, he effectively had no nationality—his Hong Kong travel documents had expired, and he hadn't applied for U.S. citizenship. China had just opened up, and the state felt conditions for overseas talent to return were not yet mature, with policies being unclear. There was no suitable environment for research domestically, and relevant departments suggested that he could be more useful by staying abroad. He said that if one returns but cannot conduct research, it does the country no good, yet many fail to consider this reality. Therefore, the choice facing Wang and Deng today is the same: one must consider both whether it benefits the country and whether it is conducive to the mathematician's own academic progress. If they return only to face endless troubles and cannot accomplish anything, there is no point. So, what would they encounter first upon returning? The first hurdle is whether they can become academicians. In China, seating is always arranged by rank and title; academicians sit on the stage, and non-academicians sit below. The selection process for academicians follows its own independent order, not directly related to research; even with an international award, one may not necessarily obtain the academician. title. He even stated that the academician system has, to some extent, become a framework for competing for power; to help professors get elected, one must pull resources and use connections, exerting efforts far beyond academic pursuits. So every time he invites scholars of Chinese descent to return, their first question is often: if I cannot become an academician, why should I return? Besides academicians, there are "hats," such as the Changjiang Scholar title and other programs. On the surface, they are honors, but in reality, many resources and benefits are tied to these titles. Yau Shing-tung has never accepted any such "hats," nor does he need them. When he first returned to. China in 1979, he had already achieved success, so others were embarrassed to press him on whether he was an academician; but a scholar returning without such titles would surely face this issue. So why does he still encourage others to come back? Because conditions are different today, he noted that China has a cohort of excellent students and has attracted top-tier scholars. The Qiuzhen College can at least provide an environment for focused research, where respect is based on scholarship rather than titles or status. He said that for decades everyone has hoped for a Chinese scholar to win the Fields Medal, and the dream has finally come true. Even while inviting Zhang, he knew there was a high probability he wouldn't return, as he had just won the prize and faced many engagements, visits, and a great deal of pressure. He hopes these two young men will keep going, because many talented scholars lose their luster after winning major awards and, ironically, stop doing research. Jacob Tsimerman, a University of Toronto math professor who won the award alongside them, announced he was joining OPI at. the time, which Shing-Tung Yau disagreed with. He believes the most important thing for a mathematician is to continue doing math research with peace of mind. He mentioned a more practical consideration: Yitang Zhang’s current environment abroad is good, but the long term is hard to predict. As relations between China and Western developed nations grow complex, it is uncertain whether Chinese scholars will always be treated fairly. After winning his own award in 1982, he also experienced discrimination in the United States, and that was when U.S.- China relations were relatively friendly. Moving on to a more fundamental question: how exactly is a mathematician discovered, trained, and.

grown? Chinese students enter the best schools via the Gaokao—this path is smooth—but what does it take to go from undergraduate studies all the way to the Fields Medal podium? This is also the focus of much. criticism: the domestic system is better at screening than at cultivating . Shing-Tung Yau believes such screening is not necessarily done correctly, as the standards rely too heavily on the Olympiad. Those truly suited for mathematical research might not fit those criteria. Zhang is an example; he graduated high school at 16 , but due to enrollment caps in Guangxi during the Gaokao, he couldn't enter the math department. He assessed this not as cruel, but as unfair. He said that for his Shing-Tung Yau College, as long as the students are good enough, he will admit them; there is no rule on how many can be taken from any one place. Even under such difficult circumstances, he insisted on studying mathematics; many others facing the same situation would have given up long ago, but he didn't. The CAS Institute of Mathematics was once a research hub that also trained young people, but for. a time, research and education became disconnected. Tsinghua's mathematics department was merged into Peking University in the 1950s and didn't begin rebuilding its discipline until 1979, only becoming a major center again in the last decade or so. Without genuine professional training and having never met top-tier mathematicians, one wouldn't know where the important problems lie and thus couldn't conduct significant research. After Hong entered MIT and studied under a top professor, he reached his. current level; therefore, both interest and the right environment are essential . A good system should allow interested and talented students to meet good teachers, rather than relying on luck for a tiny few to struggle through on their own. Next is the statement for which he was most severely criticized. In April 2024, he gave a lecture at Huazhong University of Science and Technology titled "The Current Status and Future of Chinese Mathematics." He said that Chinese mathematics had not yet reached the level of the United States in the 1940s. This statement sparked huge controversy. He later recalled that a friend told him that day, "Tens of millions of people are criticizing you online." But he still. felt that he had to tell the truth. Whether it's an individual or a country , one can only make progress by admitting that there are areas where they fall short of others. He used a metaphor: suppose in high jump, the world record is two meters, but you keep jumping only one meter, and you claim that jumping one-point-five meters is already good enough—that's the attitude many have. So, is the gap between China and the U.S. narrowing or widening now? His judgment is that the gap still exists, but American strength is declining while China is on the rise . Whether China can succeed depends on these young people. To verify his judgment, he conducted a careful investigation and edited a book called.

"The Past and Future of Mathematics in China." What was the U.S. like in the 1940s, as written in the book? Von Neumann, Norbert Wiener, Shannon, and Turing—these individuals jointly laid the foundations for modern computer science, cybernetics, and information theory. Wiener was the founder of cybernetics; Shannon founded modern information theory; Turing was British and earned his Ph.D. at Princeton. Four pioneers of computer science gathered together; this was the America of the 1940s. How was this era formed? Shing-Tung Yau traced the clues back further; early American universities focused on teaching, and research was. not the core. In 1876, British mathematician Sylvester went to Johns Hopkins University, promoting the development of mathematical research in American universities. In 1878, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics. The real turning point was 1912, when Birkhoff proved Poincaré’s last geometric theorem. That problem was proposed by Poincaré before his death, but he couldn't complete the proof. However, Birkhoff finished it that year, and it was officially published four years later, causing a huge sensation at the time. Why was it important? Because it changed Americans 'confidence in scholarship, proving that this country, the United States, could also produce. world-class academic work. Before Birkhoff, he had never left the United States. Later, the students he trained produced groundbreaking work in fields like Morse theory, differential topology, functional analysis, and dynamical systems, allowing a single breakthrough to form a school, and that school to branch out into several important fields. So, has China’s own "Birkhoff moment" arrived? Shing-Tung Yau’s answer is not yet. When Yang Chen-ning and Lee Tsung-dao won the Nobel Prize, it inspired an entire generation of Chinese. When he was a teenager, reading Chen Shen-shen’s article on 40 years of mathematics, he felt for the first time that Chinese. people could also do world-class mathematics. He said, you can tell young people 100 times that China can do it, but they won't necessarily believe it. A truly world-class piece of work must be achieved within China for them to believe it. Devoting so much effort to establishing the Qiuzhen College is all about providing a model to show young people that world-class work can indeed be achieved on Chinese soil. What, then, is the most important sign that a country has truly become a mathematical powerhouse? He says that, first, you must cultivate top-tier mathematicians, but what matters more is exactly where knowledge is being created. It must be done locally—not. problems finished in the U.S. and brought back, nor simply following others in imitation, but forging one's own path. At the start of the 1980s, Chinese mathematics was essentially a blank slate. It wasn't that there were no good mathematicians—Hua Luogeng, Chen Jingrun, Yang Le, and Zhang Guanghou all did fine work—but overall, it was disconnected from the global frontier. Over the past 40-plus years, it has gone through several stages: from initial ignorance to learning and introduction, sending the best students abroad for training, and today, scholars like Wang Hong and Deng. Yu can produce world-class work overseas. The final and hardest step remains: producing world-class, original work right here in China. Reaching that step requires the ability to ask the right questions. The most striking originality in the work of Wang Hong and Deng Yu is that they took a significant step forward within the framework of existing problems. In 1917 , Japanese mathematician Kakeya Sōichi proposed the Kakeya conjecture, which later became an important problem in geometric measure theory. Wang Hong and his collaborators solved the three-dimensional case, and the problem Deng Yu worked on has an even deeper and longer history. Hilbert proposed the challenge of how to rigorously. derive fluid dynamics equations from fundamental physical laws and explain fluid-related phenomena. Deng Yu has made fundamental progress in solving this problem. Truly great scholars find their own problems and blaze their own trails, ultimately opening up entirely new directions, much like the 23 problems Hilbert posed in 1900, each of which influenced mathematicians for decades. When it comes to questioning, he has a blunt assessment of the Chinese mathematical community: it asks very few questions. He asks the most questions himself—having posed hundreds—and many people are now working on them, most of which are related to geometry. He describes a.

conjecture with a vivid image: it's like planting a flag in the distance. To reach that spot, your existing mathematical tools aren't enough, so you are forced to think of new methods and new tools. Thus, a conjecture is closely related to how high and how far a scholar can see. He cited the only great conjecture of the 20th century as an example, one he thought about while in prison in the 1940s, which was later solved after 30 years by a group of great mathematicians like Selberg. How did Yau Shing-Tung choose his own problems? When he was 21, Shiing-Shen Chern told him that the Riemann Hypothesis was the most important. problem in mathematics and suggested he work on it. However, he had no interest in the Riemann Hypothesis; what he liked was geometry. During his first year at Berkeley, one of his courses was General Relativity. He wondered, if spacetime were a vacuum, what would its overall geometric structure be? How could one find a spacetime that is free of matter and devoid of singularities? One day, he happened to see the Calabi Conjecture in the library, which provided him with a path to solve this problem. So, his research approach isn't to pick the most famous or difficult problem, but to find where the problem intersects with his own interests. Chinese students are often. considered to have solid technical skills and strong problem-solving abilities, but how do they transition from solving given problems to proposing important new ones? Yau Shing-Tung says it's a cultural issue. Chinese children aren't encouraged to develop the habit of asking questions from a young age, so they lack creative ability, aren't bold enough, and are afraid to question. Another big problem is that Chinese people lack interest in popular science. Popular science in the U.S. is very successful, with many prominent scientists participating, so children learn early on about the important and frontier issues in science. Chinese society has long formed a strong, reward-oriented mindset: study to change your destiny, compete to advance your schooling, and conduct research to exchange for positions and funding. That is why Chinese students can solve problems but cannot propose them. Behind this lies the issue of evaluation systems and life goals. You. can tell whether a society is willing to let a young person dedicate themselves long-term to a field with no short-term fame or profit from this. He also cited Wang Guowei's "Realms of Scholarship," quoting, "Climbing high to gaze far, seeing the horizon." But for this to hold true, you must know the preceding lines: "Last night the west wind withered the green trees." You only see far when the trees have withered. Most Chinese scholars are unwilling to give up immediate small gains and cannot look far ahead, so they rarely ask big questions or have the courage to fundamentally transform a discipline. He went on to trace the root of this problem even further. He recently saw a television interview. from about 30 years ago, where his teacher, Shiing-Shen Chern, was being interviewed at Nankai University in Tianjin. Chern remarked at the time that when foreigners arrived in Tianjin , some would curiously observe the unique insects there, whereas no Chinese scholar would take any interest in such things. He said this stems from a lack of curiosity, which is deeply rooted in the Chinese nation’s preoccupation with personal survival and family interests for over 2,000 years. He does not oppose pursuing knowledge for the benefit of one's family or society at large, but a small portion of scholars must be able to look further ahead. In ancient times, Greek scientists would debate. astrophysics in the streets after dinner, and there were similar intellectual discussions during the Wei and Jin dynasties. Throughout history, these scholar-officials have been criticized for merely engaging in " empty talk," yet such discussions, unrelated to immediate social concerns, were precisely how basic science developed—this is the "usefulness of the useless." He even offered a specific suggestion: if 20%of all research funding were allocated solely to projects driven by interest and curiosity, and researchers were encouraged to pursue them, it would lead to significant changes. He noted that while true masters of mathematics are few, well-trained mathematicians can raise the level of mathematical.

proficiency across various industries, which is also very important. This focus on practical rewards is related to China's long history of material scarcity, but now that we have achieved a moderately prosperous society, what are we still chasing? Most parents simply want their children to live a life free of trouble and climb the career ladder as high as possible. He says frankly that to change the utilitarian mindset of Chinese parents, young people, and academicians, the aspirations of the youth must change. In the past, from the top down, we have emphasized that scholarship is for serving the country and the people, which is crucial, but we rarely talk about understanding the mysteries of. the universe or pursuing truth for all of humanity. This is a type of aspiration, and we haven't talked about it enough. When an individual pursues knowledge, they must believe that some things are worth seeking—not for what they can get, but simply because they are true and because humanity ought to know them. He has been saying these things for many years; many think he is just paying lip service, but he insists on saying them anyway. So, what is he busy with every day now? How should we go about retaining a truly excellent scholar? Shing-Tung Yau says there are actually many practical problems; when some foreign teachers first returned, they didn't even know how to go see a doctor. I suddenly had a fever on. Saturday and had to wait until Monday for someone to help. There are issues with schooling for the children. One teacher from France had his wife and two kids still in France. Because the children only spoke French and couldn't move here, he ultimately had to leave China and return to France to be with his family. He said he never gives up on anything he does—he has never given up on anything in his life—and he certainly won't give up on persuading Wang and Deng to return to China.
